summary: A plaster for scrofulous and parotid swellings contains beef suet, terebinth, manna, and five ounces of the Sardian earth that fullers use.
quote: of the earth called Sardian, which the fullers use, five ounces.
note: Greek has 'σάρδης' (earth 'called sarde'), which the draft renders as 'Sardian'. Evidence that the earth was used in the fulling trade.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Urine of an uncorrupted boy with nitron and lime for callous ulcers
summary: For callous, bank-edged ('sweet') ulcers, Archigenes smears roasted nitron and unslaked lime mixed with the urine of an uncorrupted boy around them, or verdigris, frankincense, salt and honey.
quote: smear around them roasted nitron and unslaked lime with the urine of an uncorrupted boy

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Andreas' plaster, opening Asclepiades' first group
summary: First in Asclepiades' list is the plaster of Andreas: litharge 3 lb; copper scale, chalcitis and verdigris 3 oz each; vinegar 1 cotyle; old oil 8 lb. Drugs of Aster and Amphion follow.
quote: The plaster of Andreas, repressive of every excrescence.
note: Probably Andreas of Carystus, Ptolemy IV's physician (outside knowledge). An emollient of Andreas appears at K13.982.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Turpilianus' plaster 'of the philosophers'
summary: A plaster attributed to Turpilianus is called 'of the philosophers'. It is good for rheumatic and chronic ulcers and brings up corrupted bones.
quote: Turpilianus', the one called "of the philosophers".
note: Turpilianus is a Roman name; who this was is unknown.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Scribonius Largus' well-tried plaster
summary: Asclepiades includes a well-tried plaster 'of Scribonius Largus': wax 100 dr (or 50), litharge 50 dr, myrtle oil 1 kotyle, and 2 dr each of burnt misy, burnt chalcitis, burnt split alum, white lead and terebinth.
quote: Another, of Scribonius Largus, a well-tried drug.
note: Scribonius Largus, physician to Claudius, author of the Latin Compositiones (outside knowledge). 'Largus' also appears alone at K13.827-828 and K13.937-938.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Heras' praised plasters: Aribarzaneios, Isis, panacea, Hicesius
summary: Heras' book includes several much-praised plasters: the Aribarzaneios for malignant, spreading ulcers, the Isis for gangrenes, a good-coloured one, his panacea, and that of Hicesius.
quote: For all have praised both the plaster called by him Aribarzaneios, as curing malignant, spreading [751] and hard-to-heal ulcers, and the Isis, as circumscribing gangrenes
note: The name presumably honours a King Aribarzanes of Cappadocia, fitting Heras' Cappadocian origin (outside knowledge).

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Mantias' book 'The Drug-seller at the Surgery'
summary: Galen cites a book titled 'The Drug-seller at the Surgery' by Mantias, and its verdigris plaster (burnt copper, pine resin, wax, verdigris, oil, Cimolian earth, frankincense, copper scale, worked smooth with vinegar for three days). It is used for wounds and cancerous ulcers and also packed into eaten-away teeth (K13.751-752).
quote: as indeed has the one written in the book entitled Mantias' "The Drug-seller at the Surgery" (pharmakopōlēs ho kat' iatreion).
note: Mantias, a Herophilean teacher of Heraclides of Tarentum (outside knowledge). The 4 minae of burnt copper looks out of scale beside the drachm amounts.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: 'Plaster of Galen, our own': wax, pitch, bitumen base
summary: Galen's own plaster: wax, pitch and bitumen 1 litra each; manna, verdigris and white lead ½ litra each; pomegranate rind, oak-gall, Egyptian thorn, Illyrian iris, round aristolochia and chalcanthum 4 oz each; long aristolochia and burnt copper 2 oz each.
quote: Of wax, of pitch [753] and of bitumen, one litra each; of manna, of verdigris, of white lead, half of the aforesaid amount, that is, half a litra of each.
note: The heading 'Plaster of Galen. Our own, a good one.' closes K13.751-752. The dry ingredients are ground with vinegar over several days.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Galen's wax-free plaster for fistulas and Chironian ulcers
summary: Galen's own plaster without wax: litharge 3 lb, old castor oil 4½ lb, sharpest vinegar 2 lb, and 2 oz each of black copper scale, chalcitis and verdigris, boiled until it no longer stains. It closes callous fistulas.
quote: Our wax-free plaster. ♃ litharge 3 pounds, old castor oil 4½ pounds, sharpest vinegar 2 pounds, black scale of copper and chalcitis and verdigris, of each of the three 2 ounces apiece.
note: Steel scale is preferred, then black scale, then Cyprian copper scale (K13.760-761).

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Boiling Heras' panacea outdoors because of fire risk
summary: Heras' panacea ('Health') is made of herbs steeped overnight in oil, then litharge, ampelitis and asphalt boiled over a gentle fire. It must be boiled outdoors and never allowed to boil over, because once it catches fire it is hard to put out.
quote: One must take care that it never boils over, and, as far as possible, boil it in an open space, for it becomes hard to extinguish if it catches hold of anything.
note: Ingredients at K13.766-767: chamaepitys, comfrey, chamaeleon, horehound, polion, centaury, elecampane, aristolochia and others.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Isis (Epigonus' plaster): uses against venoms and wounds
summary: Heras' Isis, also called Epigonus' plaster, heals head wounds with cut bone without removal. It treats punctures, human and dog bites, and draws out venom of viper, scorpion, sea-dragon and stingray.
quote: and it draws out the venoms of viper, scorpions, sea-dragons and stingray, and is good for fractures of the limbs with a wound.
note: The recipe (wax, terebinth, red copper scale, verdigris, aristolochia, myrrh, aloe, galbanum and others) is at K13.774-775.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Epigonus freed from prison after curing a powerful man
summary: Galen reports that more accurate writers say Epigonus, shut up in prison, was released after curing one of the very powerful men. The Isis plaster is named after him.
quote: having been shut up in prison and having cured one of the very powerful men, he was released on that account.
note: A rare anecdote about Epigonus. Galen does not identify the powerful man.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Galen's teacher added dracontium to the Isis
summary: Galen always adds 8 dr of dracontium root to Heras' Isis, following one of his teachers. The teacher also used colophony instead of terebinth and kneaded the plaster at length with sharp vinegar in a bronze vessel.
quote: I myself have always used it in this way, since one of my teachers too used it, putting into the proportion written by Heras 8 drachmas of dracontium.
note: The teacher is not named.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Hermon the sacred scribe; recipe from the Hephaesteum in Egypt
summary: The same plaster is called that of Hermon the sacred scribe, and others say it came from the inner sanctuaries of the Hephaesteum in Egypt, like the dittany plaster. Galen says these are all one drug.
quote: He called it, as some others also do, the plaster of Hermon the sacred scribe. In others you would find it written that this one too is from the inner sanctuaries at the Hephaesteum in Egypt
note: Evidence that temple origins were claimed for recipes, with Egyptian priestly scribes as authorities.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Dittany 'hiera' plaster from the temple of Hephaestus at Memphis
summary: The plaster made with dittany is also called hiera, said to have been found in the temple of Hephaestus at Memphis. Heras' version uses Cretan dittany, and burnt as a fumigant it drives off venomous creatures.
quote: saying that this prescription also was found in the temple of Hephaestus at Memphis.
note: Hephaestus here corresponds to Ptah of Memphis (outside knowledge).

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Jewish asphalt and pine-wood spatula in the black Hikesios
summary: Heras' black Hikesios plaster calls for 100 dr each of litharge, Jewish asphalt and ampelitis earth, stirred with a pine-wood spatula. It treats wounds, dog-bites, indurations and dropsy.
quote: Litharge 100 dr.; Jewish asphalt 100 dr.; ampelitis earth 100 dr.
note: Dead Sea bitumen (outside knowledge).

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Manna is the shaken-off residue of frankincense
summary: Galen explains that 'manna' in recipes is the aposeisma (shaken-off residue) of frankincense, which carries a little bark and is therefore more astringent.
quote: For that is what they call [784] the shaken-off residue (aposeisma) of frankincense, which partakes also to some small degree of the bark.
note: The term is important for reading every recipe in the work.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Heras: Halieus plaster cured a stingray wound
summary: Heras says he once used the Halieus plaster (with Sinopian earth) on a man struck by a sea stingray who was in dreadful pain, and it worked marvellously; also on scorpion stings.
quote: Indeed, I once used it on someone who had been struck by a sea stingray and was suffering most dreadfully, and it worked marvellously; likewise also on those stung by scorpions.
note: The first person is Heras, quoted by Galen, not Galen himself.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Heras wrote one book (Narthex); five books of Criton survive besides Cosmetics
summary: Galen says Heras wrote a single book on drug composition, the Narthex, while five such books of Criton survive in addition to his Cosmetics.
quote: Heras composed one book on the composition of drugs, entitled Narthex. But five such books of Criton survive, apart from the Cosmetics.
note: Key evidence for the size and titles of these lost works. Criton's Cosmetics book 2 is cited at K13.1039-1040.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Herodotus, source of Criton's Hicesius recipe
summary: Criton records that he received his recipe for the Hicesius plaster from Herodotus. A 'simple willow plaster as Herodotus gives it' appears later.
quote: I received this recipe from [789] Herodotus.
note: Probably the Pneumatist physician Herodotus (outside knowledge).

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Alexandrian mina 20 ounces; ounce 7, 7½ or 8 drachms
summary: Writers on weights disagree: the mina is 16 or 20 ounces (some say the Alexandrian mina is 20 and the other 16), or 100 drachms or more, and the ounce is 7½ drachms, 7 or 8.
quote: some also making a distinction and asserting that the Alexandrian mina is twenty ounces and the other sixteen
note: Galen uses these figures to show Criton wrote the Hicesius at double Heras' quantities.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Machairion's plaster for rabid-dog bites, also taken as pills
summary: Criton's plaster of Machairion treats fresh wounds and bites of rabid dogs: applied widely, changed often, and taken as a bean-sized pill for 30 days.
quote: In cases of those bitten by rabid dogs it is excellent, applied over a wider area and changed very frequently, and taken as a pill about the size of a bean for 30 days.
note: Notable for a plaster also swallowed as a pill.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Damocrates' Dysrachitis for fistulas and gout
summary: The Dysrachitis (as Damocrates gives it, via Criton) is put into callused sinuses and fistulas. Spread widely at the start of a gout attack, it lets patients keep walking and working without bathing until the third day.
quote: It also acts wonderfully on gouty patients when it is spread on as a plaster at the beginning of the paroxysm and applied around over a broad area
note: Damocrates (Servilius Damocrates) wrote recipes in verse (outside knowledge).

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Attic kotyle = 9 Italian ounces = 60 drachms; graduated horns
summary: Galen explains that Heras' 180 drachms of oil equal three kotylai. The Attic kotyle is 9 Italian ounces measured on graduated horns, which weigh 7½ weight-ounces, or 60 drachms at 8 drachms to the ounce.
quote: for the Attic one at any rate does weigh that, being of nine Italian ounces. For the nine Italian ounces, those marked on the graduated horns, weigh seven and a half weight-ounces, which come to sixty drachms
note: Distinguishes volume ('measure') ounces from weight ounces; graduated horn measures were used for oil. Asclepiades' version of the Hicesius in External Remedies book 2 is fourfold.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Verse recipes preserve proportions better than prose
summary: Galen often says that recipes written in verse, like Damocrates', are more useful than prose because they aid memory and keep the proportions accurate.
quote: It has often been said by me that metrical writings are more useful than those written in prose, not only for memory but also for the accuracy of the proportion of the ingredients that are mixed.
note: Compare K13.995-996, where Menecrates' spelled-out numerals are said to have been undone by copyists.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Aristarchus of Tarsus' troches, also taken by mouth
summary: Asclepiades' first troche is Aristarchus of Tarsus' polychrest, for ulcers, fistulas and womb conditions. It is also swallowed, 3 obols in a suitable drink, for early phthisis, spleen, coeliac and dysentery patients.
quote: it works [825] for incipient phthisics, splenetics, coeliacs, dysenterics, being given in the weight of three obols with the appropriate drink.
note: Aristarchus' name is in the heading at the end of K13.824. The troche is taken up in Falernian wine.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Agathinus: troche with boiled egg yolks
summary: A troche from Agathinus' writings combines white lead, manna, frankincense, crocomagma, unburnt sulphur and the yolks of boiled eggs, taken up in sweet wine.
quote: From the (writings) of Agathinus. Take white lead 6 drachms; manna, frankincense, 1 drachm each; crocomagma 2 drachms; unburnt sulphur 2 drachms; yolks of boiled eggs 6 drachms
note: Agathinus, Pneumatist teacher of Archigenes (outside knowledge).

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Musa's remedy in Andromachus' pastilles
summary: Andromachus lists a remedy (iatreion) of Musa: split alum, aloe, myrrh and chalcanthum 6 dr each, saffron and krokomagma 3 dr, kytinoi 4 dr, taken up with honeyed Falernian wine.
quote: The remedy (iatreion) of Musa.
note: Possibly Antonius Musa, Augustus' physician (outside knowledge). The same unit gives the 'pastille of Darius'.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Tiberius Caesar's remedy for herpes
summary: Among troches is one 'of Tiberius Caesar' for herpes: diphryges, meconium, split alum and acacia, 3 oz each, taken up with vinegar or water.
quote: For herpetes, the one of Tiberius Caesar. ℞ Diphryges, meconium, split alum, acacia, 3 ounces each; taking up with vinegar or water, use.
note: A remedy attributed to the emperor Tiberius.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Keranitos troche: bronze mortar, or extra copper scale instead
summary: The keranitos troche is ground during the Dog-star heat in a bronze mortar with a bronze pestle. Without a bronze mortar, add a mina (100 dr) of copper scale instead, so the mortar evidently supplies copper.
quote: Grind, during the heat under the Dog-star, in a bronze mortar and with a pestle. But if you do not have a bronze mortar, put in 1 mina of scale, which is 100 dr.
note: Shows awareness that a copper vessel adds metal to the drug. The same unit names the 'Bithynian' troche 'prepared in Sicily'.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Phanias' sitz-bath for haemorrhoids in a single man's urine
summary: Phanias' sitz-bath: equal parts chalcanthum, split alum, chalcitis, raw misy and sandarach (12 dr) in two xestai of old stale urine of a single man, topped up, sat in for 7 days. The gluey sediment is smeared on the anus.
quote: put old, stale urine of a single man, 2 xestai by measure, into an earthenware basin, and 12 dr. of the drug
note: 'Of a single man' may mean from one man only; the sense is uncertain.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Melanteria prepared from nails
summary: Andromachus' golden powder for spreading sores calls for melanteria 'of the kind prepared from nails'. When fresh, as Philinus says, it works better on spreading sores.
quote: melanteria, the kind prepared from nails, 5 dr.
note: Implies melanteria made artificially from iron nails, beside the mined kind.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Asclepiades' 'Marcellas': fifth book or fourth book?
summary: Galen calls Asclepiades' fifth book of External Remedies 'Marcellas' here, but later says it is the fourth book, so the numbering is inconsistent in text or draft.
quote: of the External Remedies, which he entitles Marcellas.]
note: Compare K13.965-966 ('fourth book ... which he entitles Marcellas') and K13.1009 ('fourth book of the External remedies'). The title Marcellas presumably honours a dedicatee.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Cephalic dry remedy with silphium
summary: A cephalic dry remedy with 50 dr of silphium, plus pine resin, pumice or roasted sory, iris, aristolochia, copper scale and frankincense, melts calluses and fills ulcer hollows. Some versions leave out the silphium.
quote: The remedy with silphium. It melts away callused parts, cleanses foul parts, fills up the hollows of ulcers, and melts away the little tunics that remain.
note: Cyrenaic silphium was rare or extinct by Galen's day (outside knowledge), which may explain the versions without it.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Lucius' quince-yellow escharotic moistened with fasting saliva
summary: Lucius the teacher's escharotic: raw chalcitis 8 dr and cadmia 4 dr, barely moistened with saliva while fasting, covered until quince-yellow, dried in the shade and pressed in with the olive-tip of a probe.
quote: fasting, take it up with saliva to such an extent that the drug is only just moistened, then gather it together and, having covered it, let it become quince-yellow
note: Fasting saliva was valued as a remedy (outside knowledge: Pliny NH 28).

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Apelles' papyrus remedy, also infused for dysentery
summary: Apelles' 'papyrus' remedy (burnt papyrus, burnt lead, burnt washed copper, arsenic, steel scale, sulphur) stops and prevents spreading sores. Infused with rose oil in dysentery, a biting sensation warns of a spreading sore.
quote: And whenever, he says, on being infused into dysenteric patients it causes a biting sensation, the spreading sore is to be suspected.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Demosthenes of Massalia publishes his anthrax remedy during an outbreak
summary: The Massaliote (named Demosthenes in the next unit) made his remedy public for the city because anthrakes were rife and killing many. It is kept in a Cyprian bronze vessel and pressed on with a probe until the anthrax turns black.
quote: The remedy of the Massaliote. He set this forth publicly for the city in view of its power, because anthrakes were prevalent and were carrying off many.
note: An epidemic and a public health act in Massalia; no date is given. The ingredients are chrysocolla, roasted nitron, Asian stone, arsenic, sandarach, misy, chalcitis, alum and diphryges.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Dioscorides of Tarsus gave Areius the Asclepiadean a styptic
summary: A haemostatic that checks bleeding marvellously (chalcitis, manna, dry resin, gypsum) was given by Dioscorides of Tarsus to Areius the Asclepiadean. Gypsum is added at the time of use.
quote: And as Dioscorides of Tarsus gave it to Areius the Asclepiadean, checking haemorrhages marvellously
note: Areius is presumably the dedicatee of Dioscorides' Materia Medica, so this Dioscorides may be the pharmacologist himself (outside knowledge).

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Physicians who lost their drug stocks died of grief
summary: Galen says the method helps when drugs run out on journeys, especially by sea. Even at home, some physicians who lost their stock of drugs wasted away from grief and died.
quote: seeing that even while remaining in their own place some have lost the stock of drugs by which they used to treat those in need, so that they wasted away from grief and died.
note: Possibly an allusion to losses in the fire of 192 at Rome, which Galen describes in On the Avoidance of Grief (outside knowledge; the text names no event).

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Galen improvises drugs on journeys, refined by trial
summary: Galen often improvises drugs on journeys. Some proved as good as the most famous, after a first composition by technical conjecture and a second or third correction based on experience.
quote: just as you often see me too doing, [862] both on journeys abroad and otherwise. At any rate, some of the ones improvised in such circumstances, when tested by experience, appeared in no way inferior to the most renowned.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Criton's 'fourth book On Simple Drugs': odd title in the Greek
summary: Galen says he is quoting plasters that Criton wrote 'in the fourth book on simple drugs'. Criton's drug books dealt with compound drugs, so this title is suspect even though the draft follows the Greek faithfully.
quote: first mentioning the plasters which Crito wrote in the fourth book On Simple Drugs, in his very words.
note: The Greek reads 'ἐν τῷ δ΄. περὶ τῶν ἁπλῶν φαρμάκων'. Possibly a slip or corruption (e.g. for the fourth of his pharmacological books, cf. K13.707-708, K13.786-787), or else an otherwise unattested work. The draft is not at fault.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Hippocrates: 'moderate numbness relieves pain'
summary: Galen explains that henbane and poppy were added to the herb plaster for their numbing coldness, citing Hippocrates that moderate numbness relieves pain.
quote: And moderate numbness relieves pain, says Hippocrates.
note: Hippocratic Aphorisms 5.25 (outside knowledge).

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Criton found the 12-fold cerate dilution by stepwise trial
summary: Galen reconstructs Criton's method: he did not hit on twelvefold cerate at first but went from eightfold to tenfold to twelvefold until the drug stopped biting. This is Galen's model of conjecture corrected by experience.
quote: For if, when eightfold had been mixed in, it still appeared biting, he mixed it in tenfold; and just so, if it was still biting at tenfold, he went on to the twelvefold.
note: Galen's inference about Criton's process, not something Criton reports.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Criton's whetstone plaster: chronic pain, menses, spleen
summary: Criton's plaster 'with whetstone' is used for chronic pains, headache, gout, sciatica, toothache and liver or spleen hardness, and placed above the pubes to bring on the menses. It is very hot, containing mustard, adarke, sulphur and Cnidian berry.
quote: The plaster with whetstone (ἀκόνη), which is in use among us, is effective against all chronic conditions, and specifically against headache when applied to the forehead
note: Left on seven days (five for delicate patients) until it raises pustules.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Criton's 'Invincible': prevents hidden abscesses of colon and peritoneum
summary: Criton's 'Invincible' plaster (copper scale, pyrethrum, stavesacre, Cnidian berry, mustard, cachrys, pigeon's dung, cumin, rocket, nitron, bay-berries, fig decoction) is said to prevent hidden abscesses in the colon and peritoneum, or make them burst into the bowel.
quote: it does not allow concealed abscesses to form in the colon and the peritoneum, provided at least that suppuration has not already taken place
note: The same unit names Criton's 'Mesiane' plaster.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Serapion's plaster, called Egyptian or Aphrodite, from Criton's Pharmakitis
summary: Criton's book of drugs (Pharmakitis) gives the plaster of Serapion, also called Egyptian or Aphrodite, for wounds, punctures, parotid swellings, ulcers of the aged and Chironian ulcers. It is stored in a skin.
quote: Crito wrote this one too, in his book of drugs (the Pharmakitis), in the following words: the plaster of Serapion, which some call Egyptian, others Aphrodite.
note: Possibly the Empiricist Serapion of Alexandria (outside knowledge).

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Reason and experience compared to weather forecasting
summary: Galen says drugs found by reason are hopes confirmed by experience, and hopes differ in strength. We expect rain at the winter solstice far more than at the rising of the Dog-star.
quote: For we do not hope alike that there will be rain at the winter solstice and at the rising of the Dog-star.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Erasistratus improvised herb juice when lacking a stomatic
summary: Galen's example of improvising: Erasistratus, on a journey without a stomatic drug, made one from herb juice on the spot.
quote: as Erasistratus once found a supply of the juice of herbs when he did not have a stomatic drug with him in that place on his journey
note: A small anecdote about Erasistratus not otherwise widely attested (outside knowledge).

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Galen claims priority: no predecessor wrote a general method
summary: Galen says no predecessor wrote a general method of compounding, and none recorded a drug just for nerves pricked by needles or children's styluses, whereas he set out a great many.
quote: For the general method was written by none of my predecessors, neither accurately with distinctions nor deficiently without distinctions
note: The Greek names needles and 'τὰ γραφεῖα τῶν παιδίων' (children's writing styluses) as causes of nerve punctures. Refers back to book III of this work on nerve wounds.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Andromachus' drug books neglected by physicians
summary: Andromachus gave recipes without powers or uses, so his books, though full of excellent drugs, have rightly been neglected. The grey Egyptian plaster with sea-water for soaking the wax is the example.
quote: For this reason, then, his books on drugs, although they contain the compositions of a very great many excellent drugs, have with good reason been neglected by physicians.
note: This unit's automatic check failed, but the Greek 'ἠμέληνται τοῖς ἰατροῖς' supports the rendering 'neglected by physicians'.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: One in a thousand masters the art; Empiricists deny reasoning
summary: Galen says perhaps one physician in a thousand masters the art, and the rest, like laymen, just follow written recipes. Even notable Empiricists say no compound drug was found by reasoning.
quote: For among a thousand, some one person seems to possess the perfection of the art, while the rest, [892] just like laymen, are content if they are able to use correctly the drugs that have been clearly written up.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Kotyle differs by city: Attic, Alexandrian, Ephesian
summary: Andromachus, who lived in Rome, should have used litrai, xestai and ounces. The kotyle is used in Greek cities outside Italy and differs greatly between them, so the city (Attic, Alexandrian, Ephesian) must be stated.
quote: he ought to have said either 'I mean the Attic cotyle' or the Alexandrian or the Ephesian or some other.
note: Most writers on measures say the physicians' kotyle is 9 Roman ounces; others say 12; Galen heard one claim 16.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Galen weighed the Roman oil litra: 12 measure-ounces = 10 weight-ounces
summary: In Rome Galen weighed the oil litra, which is measured with graduated horns, on a balance and found that 12 measure-ounces of oil weigh 10 weight-ounces. He urges physicians to say whether they mean measure or weight.
quote: I, at any rate, in Rome once weighed the so-called litra of oil, which they measure by means of the graduated horns
note: Direct metrological experiment by Galen. He adds that he gave the weights of liquids in another treatise (perhaps the lost or spurious De ponderibus; outside knowledge).

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Galen's rule: weight-litra of litharge to measure-litra of oil
summary: From much boiling, Galen finds the right mixture is equal weight-litra of litharge and measure-litra of oil. More oil boiled longer makes it more drying. For white plasters, white lead is added and less oil used because long boiling blackens litharge.
quote: the well-proportioned mixture of it comes about when the weight-litra of litharge is set equal to the measure-litra of oil

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Galen uses Sicyonian oil or improvises one with roots
summary: Galen often used Sicyonian oil in discutient plasters. When none was available he made a similar oil by boiling roots of wild cucumber, bryony and marshmallow in it.
quote: I myself have often put Sicyonian oil into the discutient plasters, and when that too was not available, I improvised another oil
note: Castor oil may be replaced by old oil (same unit).

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Galen inferred the Egyptian plaster's uses before reading Asclepiades and Criton
summary: Galen worked out the uses of Andromachus' grey Egyptian plaster from its ingredients and confirmed them by trial. Only later did he come across the drug books of Asclepiades and Criton, which state its powers.
quote: when I also came upon the pharmacological books of Asclepiades and Criton, I learned that they had written, not indefinitely as Andromachus too had done, but with distinctions
note: Shows when Galen first read these sources.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Damocrates' Tyrian plaster takes on Tyrian purple colour
summary: Damocrates' bandage-free Tyrian plaster (litharge 5 lb, wax 1, pine resin 3, verdigris, galbanum, burnt copper, scale, rich oil) takes on the colour of Tyrian purple when properly made. It checks eye fluxes when placed on the forehead.
quote: I call it the Tyrian, for it takes on the colour of Tyrian purple, if it is made in the way it ought.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Altering a recipe slightly to claim it as one's own
summary: Damocrates notes that some people, wanting the drug named after them, change it slightly, dropping steel scale and using sixteen drachms of copper scale.
quote: But some, wishing this drug to be called their own, remove the one [922] of the one scale and put in the sixteen
note: The draft's 'remove the one of the one scale' is garbled; the sense seems to be swapping steel scale for copper scale.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Clemens Sertorius cured of a bronchocele
summary: Andromachus records a discutient plaster for bronchoceles and indurations 'with which Clemens Sertorius was cured' (litharge, pine resin, old oil, galbanum, burnt copper, ammoniac, alum, manna, wax).
quote: Another discutient for bronchoceles, with which Clemens Sertorius was cured, and for indurations
note: A green akopon 'according to Clemens Sertorius, which I use' appears at K13.1037. The draft marks a 'wax 50 pounds (?)' figure in this unit as doubtful.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Plaster with ash of asps for scrofula and gout
summary: A discutient plaster for scrofulous swellings and gout contains 140 dr of ash of asps with terebinth, Asian stone, asphalt, aphronitron, bay-berries, pyrite, quicklime. The ash goes in last, once cooled, or the drug is ruined.
quote: Another, the one made with asps, dispersive of scrofulous swellings and for gout.
note: This unit's automatic check failed.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: 'Of Codamus, or of King Nicodemus': drawing plaster
summary: A drawing plaster (wax, red nitron, roasted resin, ammoniac, propolis, oak mistletoe, lye) is attributed 'to Codamus, or to King Nicodemus'.
quote: Another, of Codamus, or of King Nicodemus.
note: This unit's automatic check failed. 'King Nicodemus' is otherwise unknown and may be a corruption of Nicomedes of Bithynia (conjecture). The same unit has a garbled 'litharge, ??1 drachmas'.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Antonius the root-cutter's black emollient
summary: A black drawing plaster for scrofula, parotid swellings and joint complaints is given 'as Antonius the root-cutter used it': mined salt, litharge, 4 lb of pure strigil-scrapings and galbanum.
quote: It is also a good emollient (malagma), [935] as Antonius the root-cutter used it.
note: This unit's automatic check failed. Strigil-scrapings (gloios) from bathers were a drug ingredient.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Ulpianus, a gifted young man, used Damocrates' lime plaster
summary: Damocrates' discutient plaster with quicklime disperses scrofula, reduces oedema, treats watery liver and spleen, increases urine and relieves chronic sciatica. Ulpianus, a naturally gifted young man, helped very many with it.
quote: Ulpianus, a naturally gifted young man, by using this benefited very many.
note: The Greek spells the name Οὐλβιανός, which the draft normalises to Ulpianus. Damocrates' verse; the 'father of the drug' in the next unit (K13.944-945) is presumably Ulpianus.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Book heading 'BOOK 8' should be Book VII
summary: The draft renders the heading at K. XIII 946 as Book 8, following the printed Greek Η. The work has seven books, so this is Book VII.
quote: GALEN, ON THE COMPOSITION OF DRUGS BY KIND, BOOK 8.
note: The printed numbering seems shifted: Ε at 763, Ζ at 859 (draft 'BOOK 6'), Η at 946. In true Greek numerals Ζ = 7 and Η = 8, so at least one heading is misnumbered.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Fats follow animal temperament; pig's fat for soft bodies
summary: Fat takes on its animal's temperament: lion's is strongest, then leopard's, goose's and hen's. Pig's fat is softest and suits women, children, eunuchs and soft-living men raised in the shade.
quote: so that it suits tender bodies, such as those of women and children and eunuchs and of delicately-living men, bodies made effeminate by rearing in the shade, by lack of exercise, and by rather frequent baths of fresh waters.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Pale-yellow Pamphylian storax reserved for the emperor
summary: The best storax is pale yellow, finest from Pamphylia, and scarce, so it is kept for antidotes and always used when preparing anything for the emperor or a patron willing to pay. Others get the best greyish kind.
quote: so that when preparing anything with storax for the emperor at any rate you will always use this one.
note: Evidence that drug grades were matched to the patient's rank and purse. The 'emperor' is presumably Galen's imperial patron.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Scythian bdellium better than Arabian
summary: For softening, Scythian bdellium is far better than Arabian, especially fresh and soft, which recent physicians call 'fatty' or 'moister'.
quote: that the Scythian is far better for these purposes than the other, the Arabian, and especially when it is fresh and soft, which they also call "fatty" (λιπαρόν).

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Galen warns future researchers against hasty grading
summary: Galen says grading emollients into four orders needs much experience on many bodies. Any successor as industrious and truth-loving as he should not judge rashly from two or three uses, and should test on the best specimens.
quote: and so, if after me anyone should arise who is, like me, industrious and zealous for truth, let him not make pronouncements rashly on the basis of two or three uses.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Mnaseas' plaster: old oil, litharge, pig's fat
summary: Everyone agrees Mnaseas' emollient plaster is made of old oil, litharge and pig's fat, but quantities and the age of oil and fat vary. Galen counts the resulting strengths, and many say Mnaseas used equal parts.
quote: since all who have mentioned it agree with one another that it is made from old oil, litharge and pig's fat
note: Mnaseas was a Methodist physician (outside knowledge). Andromachus listed it as eleventh of his quince-yellow plasters, adding 'soft' (K13.964-965).

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Marcus Telentius Asclepiades; 'Asclepiadeion' after Asclepiades of Bithynia
summary: A malagma of Marcus Telentius Asclepiades for swellings of the womb is called 'Asclepiadeion' because it is traced back to Asclepiades the Bithynian.
quote: the drug is inscribed 'Asclepiadeion' because it is referred back to Asclepiades the Bithynian.
note: The Greek may show a different first name or spelling than 'Telentius'; check the unit.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Aquilia Secundilla: patient of Neapolites
summary: Asclepiades records a malagma 'of Neapolites prepared for Aquilia Secundilla'. A perfumed akopon composed for her appears later (K13.1030-1031).
quote: Another, that of Neapolites; it was prepared for Aquilia Secundilla.
note: A named Roman woman, otherwise unknown.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Callinicus' malagma from the writings of Paccius
summary: A malagma of Callinicus, taken from Paccius' writings, contains henbane seed, poppy juice, white poppy seed and pine nuts.
quote: Another malagma, of Callinicus, from the writings of Paccius, for all conditions.
note: Paccius Antiochus, a pharmacologist under Tiberius (outside knowledge).

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: 'For those lacking foreskin, of Epidaurus'
summary: Andromachus lists a malagma 'for those lacking foreskin, of Epidaurus' (thapsia root, pepper, calf's suet, frankincense, balsam-wood, resin, wax). Both the indication and 'Epidaurus' as an author's name are odd.
quote: Another, for those lacking foreskin, of Epidaurus.
note: Probably for 'lipodermoi' (men lacking foreskin), linked to foreskin restoration (outside knowledge). Check the Greek.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Bacchius' malagma used by Caesar
summary: Andromachus records a malagma of Bacchius 'which Caesar used': pig's fat, wax, elecampane, aromatic reed, panax root, salt, bdellium, ammoniac, rush flower, iris, frankincense, pepper, galbanum.
quote: Another malagma, of Bacchius, which Caesar used.
note: Which Caesar is not said.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: How tophi and kidney stones form
summary: Strongly heating and drying drugs disperse the thin part of a thick, viscous flux and leave the rest hardened. Galen says this is how tophi form in arthritis and stones in kidney disease.
quote: And it is in this way that in arthritic affections the tophi (poroi) come about, and in nephritic affections the stones.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Physicians' ignorance turns erysipelas into scirrhus
summary: Violently cooling and astringent drugs produce scirrhi. Galen says many patients have scirrhous tumours left from erysipelas because their physicians treated it ignorantly.
quote: And we see many people who, from erysipelas that have suffered these things immoderately, have scirrhous [994] tumours, through the ignorance of the physicians who treated them.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Menecrates' book 'Autokrator hologrammatos'
summary: Menecrates, inventor of the 'dia chylon' plaster, wrote a book titled 'Autokrator hologrammatos': dedicated to the emperor, with every number spelled out in full words, not numerals.
quote: The book in which the drug is written up is entitled 'Autokrator hologrammatos' (The Emperor, in Whole Letters): 'Autokrator' because it has been dedicated to him
note: Menecrates, physician to Tiberius or Claudius (outside knowledge). Key evidence on how recipe texts were transmitted.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Deliberate falsification of numerals by envious copyists
summary: Menecrates spelled out numbers because numerals get corrupted by accident and on purpose: the envious turn omicron into theta, or iota into another letter, by adding or scraping strokes. Later copyists put the numerals back, defeating him.
quote: who make the letter omicron a theta by drawing another, transverse, line through the middle of the round stroke
note: The Greek reads 'ἐκ τοῦ γράμμα καὶ ῥῶ', presumably a corruption of γάμμα, as the draft notes. Galen concludes that Damocrates' verse texts are more reliable (K13.995-996).

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Damocrates: young physicians hide behind elaborate cataplasms
summary: For wounds with spreading inflammation, Damocrates warns against variegated cataplasms. Young physicians use them so as to give slanderers no grounds for accusation, but a confident practitioner should share the patient's fears instead of waiting on fortune.
quote: For it is the custom of the young to do this, so that, having escaped the peaks of the inflammations, they may not furnish the slanderers with a cause of accusation.
note: The Greek 'συκοφάνταις' means 'false accusers' and is rendered 'slanderers'.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Menecrates' 'dia chylon' with mallow, fenugreek and linseed
summary: Menecrates' plaster 'through juices': oil 7 litrai in summer (9 in winter), litharge 6, plus a decoction of fresh wild mallow root (3 litrai), fenugreek and burnt linseed (½ xestes each) in 8 xestai of water, boiled until quince-yellow.
quote: Of fenugreek he said a half part of a xestes, and the same of burnt linseed. And of wild mallow he said three litrai by weight, of the root still having its fresh juice
note: Ancestor of the long-lived diachylon plaster (outside knowledge).

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: History of oils: castor oil ancient in Egypt; radish, mustard, sesame oils
summary: Olive oil was once the only oil. Castor oil came later 'among you' but was ancient in Egypt, followed by radish, mustard and sesame oils; 'among us' lily, mastic and lentisk oils and perfumed unguents.
quote: but later castor oil was added to it, among you at any rate. For in Egypt this too was ancient, and after castor oil again others, radish oil and mustard oil and sesame oil
note: Contrasts 'among you' and 'among us', apparently Italy/Rome against Galen's Greek East; the reference is not certain.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Themison used Asclepiades' first akopon
summary: Asclepiades' first akopon, from book 4 of External Remedies (marjoram, libanotis, fenugreek, cardamom, savin, sweet wine, Venafran oil, wax), is said to have been used by Themison.
quote: Themison used it. The drug is exceedingly good.
note: Themison of Laodicea, founder of Methodism (outside knowledge). The akopon is finished with Venafran oil (K13.1009-1010).

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Bassus, paralysed, saved by his own akopon
summary: Two akopa are linked to Bassus, who was paralysed for a long time and recovered after using them (myrtle and henna oils, chalcanthos, wax, terebinth, galbanum, bryony, verdigris, pepper, pyrethrum, kid's fat, euphorbium).
quote: Another, a successful drug of Bassus. He himself, having used this, after having previously been paralysed, was saved.
note: A 'Bassus the Stoic' appears at K13.1033; whether he is the same man is unknown.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Patroclus, freedman of Caesar: anointing for gout
summary: An anointing salve for gout and arthritis was compounded for Patroclus, a freedman of Caesar, to be used daily: morning before the bath, after the bath and towards evening.
quote: Another anointing-salve, the one compounded for Patroclus, freedman of Caesar; it frees the patient from the whole condition.
note: Patroclus, a known imperial freedman (outside knowledge; Suetonius and Martial mention a Patrobius/Patroclus).

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Salve for Domitius Nigrinus with seal fat
summary: A gout salve compounded for Domitius Nigrinus uses many perfumed oils, mandrake and colocynth, and six ounces of seal fat, with very old deer marrow as the substitute.
quote: of seal fat six ounces—if this is not available, one must use very old deer marrow
note: Domitius Nigrinus is named at the start of the unit.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Patron names inconsistent: Sabernius/Aburnius Valens; Pompey/Pompeius Sabinus
summary: The 'Podarces' akopon is said to be prepared for Sabernius Valens and called 'Pompey's sumptuous'. Later the 'costly' one of Pompeius Sabinus is prepared for Aburnius Valens, so one name or both seem corrupt.
quote: This preparation is to be used following upon the Podarces prepared for Sabernius Valens, which is entitled [1022] 'Pompey's sumptuous'.
note: The Greek at K13.1021-1022 reads 'Σαβερνίῳ Οὐαλέντι ... Πομπηίου πολυτελής'. At K13.1026-1027 the draft has 'Pompeius Sabinus ... Aburnius Valens'. Probably one man, Aburnius Valens (a Roman jurist of that name is known; outside knowledge).

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Killing a land tortoise for its blood with a two-edged reed
summary: In the black-poplar akopon, saffron unguent is taken up in the blood of a land tortoise, killed at the collar-bone with a reed sharpened on both sides. More blood improves the drug.
quote: The tortoise is slaughtered at the collar-bone with a reed sharpened on both sides.
note: Tortoise blood recurs in the Halieus and Valerius Paulinus akopa (K13.1025, K13.1026-1027).

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: An athlete of the xystos cured with the toad akopon
summary: An athlete of the xystos used the toad akopon as both akopon and malagma and was freed of his whole condition. Large toads are sealed in a woven basket and boiled in the oil until they dissolve.
quote: A man of the xystos (an athlete) used this both as an akopon and as a malagma, and was delivered from the whole condition.
note: The basket method is at K13.1023-1024.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Halieus cured himself of a disabling condition; recipe passed to Valerius Paulinus
summary: Halieus, so afflicted that his body was distorted, cured himself with his akopon (Sabine oil, black poplar shoots, perfumed oils, fats, sulphur, galbanum, blood of ten tortoises) and gave the recipe to Valerius Paulinus, who altered it.
quote: in which Halieus, passing his time and being gripped by the affection to such a degree that his body was distorted, used the drug and was freed from the whole condition.
note: This unit's automatic check failed. 'Passing his time' is unclear and may hide a place name or occupation.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Flavius Clemens' akopon: gout-crippled men walked again
summary: Flavius Clemens' akopon (Sabine oil, wild cucumber root, wax, terebinth, deer marrow, galbanum, six frogs) is said to have made men contorted all over by gout of feet and hands walk about unmaimed.
quote: We know of men contorted in the whole body by podagra and cheiragra who, having used this, were saved to such an extent that they walked about unmaimed.
note: Flavius Clemens is a name borne by Domitian's cousin, the consul of 95 (outside knowledge); the identification is not certain.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Celer the primipilarius: royal myrakopon prepared for him
summary: A royal perfumed akopon with Troglodytic myrrh, Falernian wine and some fifteen perfumed oils, boiled 'in the manner of perfumers', was prepared for Celer the primipilarius (senior centurion).
quote: The drug is exceedingly good; it was prepared for Celer the primipilarius.
note: A military patient.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Arruntius Aquila cured with an euphorbium akopon
summary: An akopon with opopanax, galbanum, castoreum, white pepper, euphorbium, oesypum, cassia, deer marrow and several oils is recorded as having cured Arruntius Aquila, for sciatica and sinew tension.
quote: Another acopon, with which Arruntius Aquila was cured; effective for sciatica and for every tension of the sinews.
note: The same unit gives the akopon of Glytus 'as Philoxenus the grammarian' records it.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Orion the hair-dresser's akopon with lion's fat
summary: Andromachus records an akopon of Orion the hair-dresser: wax, propolis, iris, terebinth, opopanax, oils, deer marrow, oesypum, calf's fat, lion's fat and opobalsam.
quote: Another akopon, that of Orion the hair-dresser, a good one.
note: A drug credited to a tradesman. The next recipe uses crocodile fat.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Perfumed akopon with lion's and crocodile fat
summary: Andromachus' own perfumed akopon uses aromatised goose, bull, lion and crocodile fats with deer marrow, sal ammoniac, pepper, frankincense, cinnamon, Alexandrian malabathrum and opobalsam.
quote: of aromatised lion's fat 2 ounces; of aromatised crocodile fat 1 ounce; of deer marrow 1 ounce

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Criton's Cosmetics book 2: gleukinon; Andromachus' unclear keramion
summary: Criton gave gleukinon (must-oil) in book 2 of his Cosmetics. Galen notes that Andromachus' 40-day gleukinon gives no method and does not say how many Italian litrai or xestai his keramion holds.
quote: Preparation of gleukinon, as Criton gives it in the second book of the Cosmetics.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Limnesion sold in Italy as 'adarke'
summary: Damocrates says the rough limnesion is what sellers and buyers of ingredients in Italy call adarke.
quote: and equal to these of rough limnēsion—those who sell the ingredients in Italy, and those who buy them, call this adarkē
note: Evidence of trade names in the Italian drug market.

title_work: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
title: Fire-free perfumed akopon for a king and Augustus
summary: For 'a king and Augustus' Damocrates makes a perfumed akopon without fire: about 3 oz opobalsam, 15 oz malabathrum, 15 oz cinnamon and 10 dr of odourless white wax, worked in a silver bowl over hot water and kept in silver or thick glass.
quote: But when making a myrakopon (perfumed akopon) for a king and Augustus, prepare this most easily and without fire, containing a measure of opobalsamum of about three ounces
note: Silver-bowl method at K13.1057.

title_work: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
title: Galen cites On the Elements according to Hippocrates and Causes of Symptoms
summary: For his account of how pain arises Galen refers to two of his own works, On the Elements according to Hippocrates and the Causes of Symptoms.
quote: it has been stated by me both in the work On the Elements according to Hippocrates
note: Galen's De elementis ex Hippocrate and De symptomatum causis. The draft points out that the Greek title has its words in a disturbed order.

title_work: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
title: Galen contrasts his useful exegesis with other commentators' sophistry
summary: Galen says other exegetes fill their commentaries with sophistical questions that are useless for practice. He chooses instead to add useful teaching that follows from Hippocrates' doctrines.
quote: for they sow their exegeses with sophistical questions that are of no use to learners toward the end of the art

title_work: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
title: Barley or bitter-vetch fomentation: pound, boil in oxycrate, bag
summary: Galen explains that the barley and bitter vetch of Hippocrates' fomentation are pounded before being boiled in vinegar and water and sewn into bags. Bran is prepared the same way, and bitter vetch cuts thick humours.
quote: Both barley and bitter vetch he bids one boil in vinegar and water not as whole seeds, but having first pounded them
note: The lemma says the vinegar mixture should be 'a little sharper than one would drink it'. In K15.524-525 Galen explains this middle strength: inflamed parts cannot bear pungent oxycrate.

title_work: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
title: Anatomical Procedures book III and Anatomy of Veins and Arteries
summary: On the elbow veins cut in venesection Galen refers to the third book of his Anatomical Procedures and to a separate single book on the anatomy of veins and arteries.
quote: these have been sufficiently discussed both in the third book of the Anatomical Procedures and in the Anatomy of the Veins and Arteries, written separately in another single book
note: De anatomicis administrationibus III and De venarum arteriarumque dissectione.

title_work: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
title: Azygos vein origin differs between animals and humans
summary: Galen says the unpaired vein that feeds the lower eight ribs branches off above the heart in some animals. In others, humans included, it branches off where the vena cava meets the right auricle.
quote: a single unpaired (azygos) vein, which in some animals grows off above the heart
note: This comparative anatomy comes from Galen's own dissections.

title_work: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
title: Colour change of blood as limit of venesection
summary: Blood is let until its colour changes: redder if the body's blood is phlegmatic, livid or blackish if it is red. If the patient's strength cannot bear that much, Galen says it is better to stop than to break down the faculty.
quote: it is more fitting to refrain from breaking down the faculty than from evacuating the excess blood

title_work: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
title: Aromatic seeds added to purgatives to protect stomach mouth
summary: Fragrant additives are mixed with black hellebore or peplion (daucus, seseli, cumin, anise, silphium juice) so that the purgative does not touch the sensitive mouth of the stomach unmixed.
quote: the admixture of the aromatic substances was devised, so that the power of the purgative drugs might not touch the mouth of the stomach by itself and unmixed
note: The lemma (K15.535-536) lists the additives. This unit's checks verdict is 'fail'.

title_work: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
title: Purgatives known by experience, need for purging by reason
summary: Galen refers to his books On the Power of Simple Drugs: which humour a purgative draws is learned by experience, while the need to purge downward-tending humours was found by reason and confirmed by experience.
quote: That the cathartic drugs are discovered through experience—both which humour each purges and whether it purges at all—you have learned in the books on the power of simple drugs
note: This is the De simplicium medicamentorum temperamentis ac facultatibus.

title_work: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
title: Hiera made with colocynth; best version has hellebore, no scammony
summary: Among purgatives Galen names the colocynth preparation that people now call hiera. Of its several versions he judges best the one that contains hellebore but no scammony.
quote: among which is also the one made with colocynth, which they now customarily call hiera.
note: K15.540 continues: 'the one that has received hellebore but does not contain scammony is the finest drug'.

title_work: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
title: Contemporary physicians overfeed after evacuation
summary: Galen says most physicians of his day feed patients abundantly after evacuating them. Hippocrates gives less ptisan after purging, because the exhausted faculty cannot work up much food.
quote: For these, whenever they have evacuated, feed abundantly

title_work: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
title: Physicians dry patients out 'like salt-fish' before feeding
summary: Galen attacks physicians who starve patients for two or three days at the start of a disease and then switch abruptly to gruels. He compares this to pickling fish.
quote: as if curing them like salt-fish, for two or three days or even more
note: In K15.594-595 Galen glosses ταριχεύεσθαι as excessive drying from untimely fasting.

title_work: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
title: Aristotelians call self-evident premises 'axioms'
summary: Analysing Hippocrates' argument as a syllogism, Galen notes that the followers of Aristotle call premises credible in themselves 'axioms'.
quote: which premises it is in fact the custom of the followers of Aristotle to call axioms

title_work: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
title: Asian Greeks still say 'greenish' for pale-yellow
summary: To explain Hippocrates' 'greenish' urine, Galen cites a usage still current among the Greeks of Asia. They call a sallow person chlōros, using it the same as ōchros.
quote: by 'greenish' he speaks according to a certain usage of the Greeks in Asia, which is preserved even now
note: This is evidence for spoken Greek in Galen's home region of Asia Minor.

title_work: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
title: Accent of ōchra (ochre) noted
summary: Galen defines the pale-yellow colour by the pigment ochre and notes that the word is accented with an acute on the first syllable.
quote: such as that of what is called ōchra (ochre), the name being accented with an acute on the first syllable

title_work: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
title: Variant reading spatilē versus asē
summary: Galen reports that many copies of Hippocrates read asē (restless distress) instead of spatilē (liquid stool). He explains what each reading would mean.
quote: but in many of the copies you will find written not spatilē [556] but asē (restless distress)

title_work: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
title: Most commentators read 'sleep after dinner'; Galen says after lunch
summary: Galen disagrees with most earlier commentators, who took the advice to sleep 'as if passing the night' to mean after dinner. He argues from the context that it means after the midday meal and offers an emendation.
quote: after dinner, as most of the commentators say, but, as the sense of what has been said requires, after the midday meal
note: In K15.557-558 he gives the corrected wording, 'one must sleep... after the luncheon'.

title_work: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
title: Paulus the rhetor: phlegmatic, vomited yellow bile daily
summary: Galen's example of a man 'bitter-bilious in the upper parts' is Paulus the rhetor. He had a phlegmatic habit of body, yet yellow bile rose every day and he vomited it after his bath, and his stools held little bile.
quote: For in Paulus the rhetor, who had a phlegmatic habit of the whole body, yellow bile floated up every day, and he vomited it first, after the bath, in no small quantity.
note: This passage does not identify him further. He is distinct from the Eudemus case that follows.

title_work: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
title: Eudemus the philosopher: bilious, bile passed downward
summary: The contrasting case is Eudemus the philosopher. He was bilious in temperament, his bile passed downward, he rarely vomited it, and his stools were full of bile.
quote: But in Eudemus the philosopher, who was bilious in temperament, it passed downward through the seat
note: Most likely the Peripatetic Eudemus whom Galen treated in Rome (On Prognosis).

title_work: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
title: Stool frequency of Eudemus versus Paulus
summary: Galen reports that Eudemus went to stool two or three times a day, while Paulus sometimes passed nothing at all. He explains this by where each man's bile went.
quote: Hence Eudemus went to stool twice each day, and sometimes even three times, whereas Paulus at times did not excrete at all.

title_work: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
title: Bile duct sometimes has a branch into the stomach
summary: Galen explains why yellow bile rises in some people: the duct from the liver to the outgrowth of the stomach is built differently in some, with a branch reaching the stomach.
quote: For sometimes in some people a branch from it reaches the stomach; in these, then, the bilious residue floats up above
note: This is an anatomical variant of the bile duct based on dissection.

title_work: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
title: Synkomistos bread now called autopyros
summary: Hippocrates' synkomistos bread, made with the bran left in, is what people of Galen's day call autopyros.
quote: people nowadays call such bread autopyros, since the branny flour in it is not separated out but is kneaded up together with the pure

title_work: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
title: Potainia: Ionic word for fresh barley-groats
summary: Galen notes that Hippocrates calls fresh barley-groats potainia, in the dialect of the Ionians and the older writers.
quote: he called the fresh ones potainia in the dialect of the Ionians and of the older writers

title_work: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
title: Empiricist 'syndromes' cannot capture degrees of illness
summary: Galen argues that teaching by the Empiricists' syndromes cannot work, because the degrees of strength, fever and sputum cannot be written down. The physician has to weigh them himself in each case.
quote: it is not possible to conduct the teaching according to what the Empiricists call syndromes.

title_work: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
title: Therapeutic Method gives the orderly teaching Hippocrates lacked
summary: Galen refers readers to his Therapeutic Method for the ordered treatment of quantity of food. He excuses Hippocrates' disorder because Hippocrates was the first to discover these things.
quote: All such matters have been stated in the treatise on the therapeutic method, in sequence and in order
note: This is the Methodus medendi.

title_work: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
title: Part 'after the bath' published posthumously from Hippocrates' notes
summary: Galen suggests that the section after the bath may be notes Hippocrates wrote for himself, found in his house and published after his death. As a treatise it is unworthy of him, like On Diseases and On Affections.
quote: if someone, having found it in the house, published it after the man's death as things written by him in outline
note: This is the so-called Appendix to Regimen in Acute Diseases.

title_work: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
title: Galen promises commentaries on On Diseases and On Affections
summary: Galen says he will settle whether On Diseases and On Affections are authentic in commentaries written on those works.
quote: we shall define this same point and decide it in the commentaries written on them
note: No Galenic commentaries on these works survive. They may have been planned only or are lost.

title_work: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
title: Books On Difficulty of Breathing cited
summary: Galen refers to his books On Dyspnoea, where he set out the causes of all kinds of laboured breathing with demonstrations.
quote: in which we have written out the causes both of these and of the other dyspnoeas together with their proper demonstrations
note: This is De difficultate respirationis in three books. It is cited again at K15.793-794.

title_work: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
title: Prognostic, On Humours and Aphorisms commentaries written earlier
summary: Galen says that before this commentary he had already expounded the Prognostic, On Humours and the Aphorisms. He also refers to his books On Crises.
quote: For we have already expounded, before this book, both the Prognostic and the work On Humours and the Aphorisms
note: This is evidence for the relative order of Galen's Hippocratic commentaries.

title_work: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
title: Layman who feeds a starved patient seems to raise the dead
summary: If a physician fails to see that a patient is weak from starvation, another physician or a layman who feeds him looks as if he had raised a dead man. Galen says such errors bring the craft into contempt.
quote: for the physician or layman who came in seems to them as if he had even raised up a dead man.

title_work: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
title: Reading anōterō versus exōterō argued letter by letter
summary: Against interpreters who take 'still earlier' as days 7 to 9, Galen argues that they would then have to write ἐξωτέρω, with epsilon and xi, not ἀνωτέρω.
quote: these people ought, if this was what pleased them, to write the beginning of the word with the letters epsilon and xi, ἐξωτέρω, and not ἀνωτέρω with alpha and nu.
note: This unit's checks verdict is 'fail'.

title_work: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
title: Book found in drafts; notes on front and back of sheet
summary: Galen explains the book's disorder: it was found in draft form after Hippocrates' death. Examples he added on the front and back of the sheet were put in the wrong places by the copyist.
quote: the examples that he had found were written in addition into the book by Hippocrates himself, for the confirmation of the universal statement, some on the front of the sheet and some on the back
note: The Greek is ἐπὶ τοῦ μετώπου / κατὰ τοῦ νώτου. This is evidence for ancient ideas about how texts were transmitted. Checks verdict is 'fail'.

title_work: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
title: Five differences of wine: colour, taste, consistency, smell, power
summary: Galen faults Hippocrates' list of wines as disordered and incomplete and sets out five kinds of difference. The colours are white, black, tawny, yellow and red.
quote: another is the quality according to taste, a third according to consistency, a fourth according to smell, and a fifth according to power.

title_work: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
title: Theraean and Scybelite: outstandingly sweet, thick, black wines
summary: Galen's examples of sweet wines are the Theraean and the Scybelite, both thick and black.
quote: At any rate the Theraean and the Scybelite are sweet wines to an outstanding degree, both being thick and black

title_work: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
title: Maeonian sweet wines: Therinos and Karyinos
summary: Sweet wines are also made in Maeonia, the Therinos and the Karyinos. They are less sweet, thick and black than the Theraean and the Scybelite.
quote: sweet too are those produced in Maeonia, the Therinos and the Karyinos

title_work: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
title: Hepsēma and siraion: boiled-down must
summary: Galen describes hepsēma and siraion, made by boiling down must. The sweeter it becomes, the blacker and thicker it is, and over-boiled must turns bitter.
quote: what is called hepsēma and siraion, which is produced from must being boiled down
note: K15.632-633 adds that must boiled too long turns bitter, as honey does.

title_work: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
title: Cough as a 'hand'; viscous phlegm clings like birdlime
summary: Galen says the breath of a cough acts like a hand that carries thick humours up, but viscous humours stick in the bronchi like birdlime. So melikraton suits thick sputa and oxymel viscous ones.
quote: And for this reason melikraton is most suitable for the thick humours with a view to expectoration, and oxymel for the viscous ones

title_work: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
title: Greek terms stryphnos (harsh) versus austēros (dry) wine
summary: Galen notes that the Greeks call an excessively astringent wine stryphnos and a more moderate one austēros.
quote: which the Greeks also call stryphnos (harsh), while they call the more moderate one austēros (dry)

title_work: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
title: Dark austere wines near Pergamum, Perperina and Aegae
summary: Not all dark wines are sweet. Galen's examples are the austere dark wines of his home region in Asia, near Pergamum and around Perperina and Aegae.
quote: some of them are austere, such as those among us in Asia near Pergamum and around Perperina and Aegae.
note: Checks verdict is 'fail'.

title_work: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
title: Cilician Anabates wine: sweet and austere at once, bad
summary: Galen says the Anabates of Cilicia combines austere and sweet qualities. For that reason it is a bad wine that lingers in the upper belly and causes wind.
quote: The Anabates in Cilicia is at once both austere and sweet, being compounded of opposite qualities
note: Checks verdict is 'fail'.

title_work: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
title: Watery wines for fever patients: Sabine, Titacazene, Tibine
summary: The best wine for the feverish is watery, white, thin and odourless. Galen's examples are the slack Sabine of Italy, which is given to fever patients, and the Titacazene and Tibine of Asia.
quote: in Italy the slack Sabine, which they also give to those with fever; in Asia the Titacazene and the Tibine.

title_work: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
title: Galen found watery wines in Cilicia, Phoenicia, Palestine, Scyros, Crete, Egypt
summary: Galen says he found thin watery wines in Cilicia, Phoenicia, Palestine, Scyros and Crete, and even in Egypt, though hot regions usually make thick strong wines. In Italy, Bithynia and Asia such wines are common.
quote: I at any rate have found wines of this kind in Cilicia and Phoenicia and Palestine and Scyros and Crete
note: This is evidence for Galen's travels (compare his journeys to Palestine and Cyprus mentioned in Simple Drugs). Checks verdict is 'fail'.

title_work: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
title: Sykota: fig-fattened livers
summary: To show that the viscera delight in sweet things, Galen points to the so-called sykota: livers that grow very large and delicious when the animal is fed dried figs.
quote: the so-called sykota (fig-fed livers) are seen, through the eating of dried figs, to become very large and most delicious
note: This is the ancient forerunner of foie gras (iecur ficatum).

title_work: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
title: Frothy, intensely bilious stools mean colliquative fever: stop melikraton
summary: Frothy, intensely bilious stools show that the fever is colliquative. Galen says to stop melikraton, move to ptisan juice, and give cold water at the right moment for the greatest benefit.
quote: know that the fever is colliquative, and on this account desist from the use of melikraton and proceed to the juice of ptisane

title_work: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
title: Sinea: Ionic for 'harms'; shown in On Fractures/Joints commentary
summary: Galen explains Hippocrates' σίνεα: the Ionians say sinein for blaptein, 'to injure'. He says he showed this in his commentary on On Fractures and On Joints.
quote: for indeed the Ionians say sinein in place of blaptein ("to injure")
note: The draft's 'treatise On Fractures and On Joints' refers to Galen's commentaries on those works.

title_work: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
title: Melikraton can stretch survival from four days to five or six
summary: Melikraton is not a weakener but a light nourishment. Galen says a fasting man who would die in four days could reach the fifth or sixth on melikraton.
quote: if someone who had fasted were going to die in four days, this person, using melikraton, could arrive not only at the fifth day but even at the sixth.
note: This answers the lemma (K15.665) that melikraton got a reputation for causing swift death through people who starved themselves to death on it.

title_work: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
title: Raw melikraton more laxative, boiled more nourishing
summary: As a side note Galen says raw melikraton loosens the bowels more, while well-boiled melikraton nourishes more.
quote: raw melikraton is more laxative, while that which has been well boiled is more nourishing

title_work: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
title: Dosage test: one kyathos of honey versus two of wine daily
summary: To compare the nourishment in honey and wine fairly, Galen describes a trial: one kyathos of honey a day against two kyathoi of wine, each diluted as the patient likes.
quote: he can, say, take one kyathos of honey either by itself or, mixing in as much water as he wishes
note: The kyathos is about 0.045 litre.

title_work: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
title: Oxymel is melikraton with a little vinegar, best boiled
summary: Galen says proper oxymel is not simply vinegar and honey but melikraton with a small amount of vinegar. Boiling it is better, because boiling weakens the vinegar's harm while keeping its benefit.
quote: For the composition of oxymel does not come about merely from a mixture of vinegar and honey, but from melikraton that takes on a small quantity of vinegar.

title_work: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
title: Holding back stool when no privy is near
summary: Galen illustrates reverse peristalsis from ordinary life. When we hold back a bowel movement because of urgent business or because no privy is near, we feel the bile run back up.
quote: or because there is no privy near at hand; for on such occasions we perceive the bile running back up in such a way that it is no longer excreted.
note: The same unit cites his commentaries On the Natural Faculties for peristalsis.

title_work: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
title: Anatomists by autopsy call the womb sinewy; hence vinegar harms it
summary: Vinegar harms sinewy parts. Nearly all anatomists, from dissection, call the womb sinewy, and Galen adds that its huge range of dilation proves it.
quote: nearly all the anatomists say that the womb is sinewy
note: This explains the lemma (K15.692-693) that vinegar is hostile to women because it pains the womb.

title_work: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
title: Erasistratus' dictum on strong powers of food and drink
summary: Galen quotes Erasistratus: strong foods and drinks bring the greatest benefit at the right moment and the greatest harm at the wrong one. He uses it to explain why physicians fall back on water.
quote: for so Erasistratus used to say: strong powers of foods and drinks, when taken at the right moment, bring the greatest benefit, but when at the wrong moment, the greatest harm.

title_work: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
title: Old man on watery wine; rival mocks 'he only looks at it'
summary: Galen tells how he gave a sick old man water with a few drops of wine each day. A visiting physician laughed that the patient was not drinking wine but only looking at it. Galen explains that wine given for benefit is mixed differently from wine given for pleasure.
quote: laughed and said that the sick man was not drinking wine [699] but only looking at it
note: Checks verdict is 'fail'.

title_work: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
title: Erasistratus' On Fevers mocks Hippocrateans' wax cups
summary: Galen says Erasistratus, in his books On Fevers, maliciously attacks Hippocrates through his pupils Apollonius and Dexippus. They supposedly made wax cups of one twelfth of a kyathos and gave fever patients one or two of them.
quote: having made twelve waxen cyathi to the cyathus that is the sixth part of the cotyle, measured out one or two of these to those suffering from fever.
note: This is a fragment of Erasistratus' lost On Fevers. It also gives a measure: the kyathos is one sixth of a kotyle. K15.744 calls these 'wax cups' (κηρίνων κυλίκων).

title_work: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
title: Apollonius and Dexippus, pupils of Hippocrates
summary: Apollonius and Dexippus are named as Hippocrates' pupils who restricted drink in fevers. Galen says Erasistratus could produce no book of theirs.
quote: Erasistratus, who mentions Apollonius and Dexippus while having no book of theirs to show
note: Dexippus of Cos is known from other sources (for example Plutarch) as a pupil of Hippocrates.

title_work: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
title: Hippocratic treatments of individual acute diseases lost or never written
summary: Galen says Hippocrates' books on treating each acute disease either do not survive or were never written. Those in circulation are not worthy of him, though they contain much of his thought.
quote: It is therefore evident either that the books written by him on the treatment of each of the acute diseases in particular are not preserved, or that they were not written at all

title_work: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
title: No public bath-houses in Hippocrates' time
summary: From Hippocrates' remarks about house equipment, smokeless shelter and plentiful water, Galen infers that bath-houses had not yet been built. Water was still heated in cauldrons at home and poured into tubs.
quote: It seems that in the times of Hippocrates these bath-houses had not yet been constructed
note: This is evidence for ancient views on the history of the bath.

title_work: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
title: Bathing in tubs in army camps without a bathhouse
summary: Galen notes that patients are still often bathed in a room with a fire and a tub of water in army camps, wherever there is no bathhouse.
