summary: Galen reminded the teacher he had bled a healthy, well-exercised man who fell from a carriage, was entangled in the reins and dragged, having only bruises; also an ophthalmia, a headache and a pleuritic.
quote: the other having fallen from a carriage and then become entangled in the reins and dragged for a considerable distance, so that certain parts were bruised
note: The teacher was left 'in the greatest perplexity'.

title_work: On Plethora
title: Planned discourse on phlebotomy
summary: Galen defers the full set of indications for bleeding to his discourse on phlebotomy, which no one has yet written precisely.
quote: I, since I have at present no leisure for idle talk, have decided not now, but in the discourse on phlebotomy
note: Probably De curandi ratione per venae sectionem (outside knowledge).

title_work: On Plethora
title: Those who make arteries and nerves 'pipes' for pneuma
summary: Galen rejects the view that faculties do not pervade solid bodies and that arteries and nerves are pipes or conduits for pneuma, refuted in PHP and Natural Faculties.
quote: who set up the arteries and the nerves as pipes or conduits for pneuma.
note: Target is Erasistratean physiology (outside knowledge).

title_work: On Plethora
title: Euexia, eusarkia, polysarkia; euaimia vs polyaimia
summary: Good nourishment of solids is euexia, increase of flesh eusarkia or polysarkia; good-bloodedness is natural in quality and quantity, much-bloodedness excess in quantity; in athletes faculty and blood rise together.
quote: in the case of blood there is on the one hand what is, as it were, a kind of good-bloodedness (euaimia), and on the other much-bloodedness (polyaimia).

title_work: On Plethora
title: Nicarchus and Praxagoras: arteries without blood
summary: Galen denies that the arterial pulse clearly shows venous plethora when thick humours block transfer, against Nicarchus and Praxagoras, who give arteries no share of blood.
quote: however much Nicarchus and Praxagoras may think so, even though they do not grant [574] the arteries any share of blood.
note: Nicarchus is obscure, perhaps a follower of Praxagoras of Cos (outside knowledge).

title_work: On Plethora
title: Skin colour reveals the predominant humour in plethora
summary: Blood plethora is deep red, yellow bile pale-yellow, phlegm whiter and black bile darker; bile in excess by itself, as in icterus, is cacochymia, not plethora.
quote: For the plethos of blood is deep red, that of yellow bile somewhat pale-yellow; and the colour turns toward whiter than the natural when phlegm predominates

title_work: On Plethora
title: Crude humour: bean-soup sediment in gluttons' urine
summary: The crude humour, thicker than phlegm, settles in urine like bean-soup sediment, especially in gluttons who avoid exercise, eat much and bathe after meals; it brings white pallor.
quote: such as settles in the urines, especially in those of people who, from gluttony, have a copious sediment resembling bean-soup
note: Only leucophlegmatic dropsy phlegm can abound through the whole body.

title_work: On Plethora
title: Sweet, sour and salty phlegm and their effects
summary: Sweet phlegm makes people somnolent, sour phlegm hungry, salty phlegm thirsty; the crude humour removes appetite; moist, cool sensory principle brings coma, dry hot brings sleeplessness.
quote: people become somnolent when the sweet kind is in excess, hungry when the sour kind is in excess, just as they become thirsty when the salty kind prevails
note: Greek: ὑπνώδεις ... ἐπὶ τοῦ γλυκέος, πεινώδεις ... ἐπὶ τοῦ ὀξέος, διψώδεις ... τὸ ἁλυκόν; draft matches.

title_work: On Plethora
title: Melancholic humour vs true black bile
summary: Black bile with acid quality makes people hungry; while it is only like a sediment of blood and not yet acid, Galen prefers to call it 'melancholic humour' rather than black bile.
quote: it is perhaps better (so far as it is called a melancholic humour) not yet to call such a humour black bile either, but, as I am accustomed, melancholic

title_work: On Plethora
title: What makes blood hotter, moister, colder, drier
summary: Idleness and moist regimen make blood moister; anger, exercise, sun exposure, rubbing, heating drugs or food, and stronger older wines make it hotter; recent chill colder; dry foods drier.
quote: from anger and exercises, from exposures to scorching heat and from rubbings, from a heating drug, from nourishment of that kind, and from wines less diluted and older, hotter

title_work: On Plethora
title: Do not diagnose plethora right after anger, bath or wine
summary: Before judging plethora from vein size and redness, wait until the effects of anger, bathing, exercise, wine or other heating have settled; then weigh heaviness, tension, pulses, sleep and appetite.
quote: it is not fitting to bring to diagnosis a man who is angry, or has bathed, or is bathing, or has exercised, or has just taken wine

title_work: On Plethora
title: Ranking of plethora signs; season, region, skin density
summary: Scientific signs (tension, heaviness, vein swelling, colour, pulse) outrank causes (suppressed excretions, idleness, rich food, baths after meals); winter, spring, cold regions and dense skin favour plethora.
quote: for in winter and spring, and in cold and temperate regions, people accumulate plethora more, but in hot and dry seasons and regions less

title_work: Against Lycus
title: Lycus' commentaries expounding Hippocrates' Aphorisms
summary: Lycus wrote exegetical commentaries (hypomnemata) on the Aphorisms; Galen says he distorts Hippocrates both where he praises and where he censures.
quote: commentaries expounding the Aphorisms of Hippocrates, but he does violence to the man's doctrines from both sides
note: Lycus of Macedon, pupil of Quintus (outside knowledge; not named here). The commentary is lost; this treatise is a main witness to it.

title_work: Against Lycus
title: Commentators of opposing sects should not expound the Aphorisms
summary: Galen holds that neither those enrolled under opposing doctrines nor those ignorant of the basics of the art are fit to expound the Aphorisms.
quote: For it is not reasonable that either those who have been enrolled under opposing doctrines, or those who do not even know the first useful things of the art, should expound the Aphorisms
note: ἐνεγράφησαν, 'were enrolled', is the language of sect membership; it implies that Lycus belonged to a rival school.

title_work: Against Lycus
title: Galen read only the opening of Lycus, then was asked to reply
summary: Galen swears he could not bear to read beyond Lycus' first expositions. He wrote this reply when a companion asked him to listen to Lycus' comment on this aphorism and many others urged him to answer.
quote: having read the first expositions of his commentaries on the Aphorisms, I could no longer bear to read the rest of the book
note: The companion asked him ἐπακοῦσαι, to listen while the text was read aloud: a detail of group reading. Galen presents the work as written on request (ἀναγκασθεὶς).

title_work: Against Lycus
title: The aphorism at issue: growing things have most innate heat
summary: Galen states the lemma under dispute: those who are growing have the most innate heat (Aphorism I.14).
quote: growing things have the most innate heat
note: Hippocrates, Aph. I.14 (outside knowledge for the numbering).

title_work: Against Lycus
title: Physicians disputed whether bodily heat comes from cardiac motion
summary: Galen reports that physicians disagree on whether heat arises from the motion of the heart and arteries or is innate in the heart, as its motion is.
quote: is a matter of dispute among physicians
note: A doxographic note on a real controversy; no names are given.

title_work: Against Lycus
title: Cites his On the Elements according to Hippocrates
summary: Galen refers readers who want a scientific proof that hot, cold, dry and wet are the principles of generation to his book On the Elements according to Hippocrates.
quote: This book is entitled On the Elements according to Hippocrates.
note: Extant De elementis secundum Hippocratem (Kühn I). Useful for relative chronology: it predates Against Lycus.

title_work: Against Lycus
title: Cites On Mixtures as following On the Elements
summary: Galen says the books On Mixtures follow On the Elements and show which bodies have more or less of the hot element, and why some are hotter or colder by nature.
quote: And following it there are others, those On Mixtures, in which I show which bodies have in themselves a greater share of the hot element
note: Extant De temperamentis (3 books). 'Following it' (ἐφεξῆς) gives a reading or composition order.

title_work: Against Lycus
title: Innate heat comes from seed and menstrual blood
summary: Everyone has the hot element innately from the first beginning, drawn from seed and menstrual blood. Individuals differ in degree within a latitude of health; beyond it they fall ill or die.
quote: For in all of us the hot element is present innately from the first beginning, which we possess from the seed and the menstrual blood.
note: The latitude (πλάτος) of health is a characteristic Galenic idea.

title_work: Against Lycus
title: Galen's own definitions of wet and dry fevers
summary: Wet fevers: the patient sweats from day one with little or no benefit. Dry fevers: violent thirst, dry tongue, skin hard as hide. Kausoi are given as dry and 'typhodeis' as wet.
quote: The patients sweat from the first day, yet are benefited by these sweats either moderately or not at all: these fevers I call wet
note: He offers his own definitions in case others use the names differently, which signals that fever nomenclature was unstable.

title_work: Against Lycus
title: Bathhouse detail: heated stone for rolling on
summary: In his analogy of well-mixed and ill-mixed baths, Galen mentions a well-tempered stone in the bath on which bathers can roll about.
quote: So at any rate a stone too becomes well-mixed in the baths themselves, one on which it is possible to roll about
note: Bath faults are listed as too cold, too hot, full of vapour, and smoky (203). Smoke differs with the fuel: oak, fig, olive (203).

title_work: Against Lycus
title: Smoke and soot distinguished by Galen
summary: Both are residues of flame. Soot (from many lamps or torches) is an earthy exhalation of over-roasted material. Smoke is from half-burnt material mixed of moist and earthy substance.
quote: soot is an earthy exhalation of material that has been roasted through, whereas smoke is neither of over-roasted material nor earthy, but of material that is half-burnt
note: Rooms lit by many lamps (λύχνων) or torch-wood are called 'sooty' (λιγνυώδη): a domestic detail.

title_work: Against Lycus
title: Lacuna before Lycus' passage on heat
summary: The text marks a gap ('Something is missing') just before Galen refers to 'this passage' of Lycus. The quoted Lycus passage itself appears to have dropped out.
quote: Something is missing.
note: Kühn prints a lacuna note. The fuller verbatim wording of Lycus' thesis survives at K18a.215-216 ('It seems to me impossible and impracticable...').

title_work: Against Lycus
title: Lycus' thesis: hot does not differ from hot
summary: Galen quotes Lycus' claim that the hot, insofar as it is conceived as hot, has no variation from another hot. He refutes it by asking what the qualifier 'insofar as' adds.
quote: ‘The hot, insofar as it is conceived as hot, has no variation with respect to another hot.’
note: A verbatim fragment of Lycus' commentary on Aph. I.14. A longer form is quoted at 215-216 (κατ’ αὐτὴν λέγω τὴν θάλψιν).

title_work: Against Lycus
title: Lycus himself wrote differences of diseases, including pleurisy
summary: Galen turns Lycus' own practice against him: Lycus wrote many differences of diseases and symptoms, including kinds of pleurisy, though 'disease does not differ from disease insofar as disease'.
quote: But Lycus himself also writes down a great many differences of diseases
note: Pleurisies differ by pain ending at the collarbone or at the hypochondrium, and by coloured sputum versus the kind some call ἄπτυστος. At 222-223 Lycus 'elsewhere writes of differences of fevers' too. Evidence for other lost Lycus writings.

title_work: Against Lycus
title: Aristotle, Theophrastus, Chrysippus, Mnesitheus on the arts
summary: Galen says these men kept Plato's view (Philebus) that the arts rest on knowing differences, and that everyone writing 'On Art' gave the same argument.
quote: and Aristotle and Theophrastus preserved his opinion, as did Chrysippus and Mnesitheus, and there is no one who did not go through the same argument in his writing On Art.
note: Mnesitheus of Athens, 4th-c. BC physician (outside knowledge), here grouped with philosophers. 'περὶ τέχνης γράμματι' may mean a genre of writings on art rather than one title. At 217 Aristotle and Theophrastus are again cited: things the same in genus can be contraries in species.

title_work: Against Lycus
title: Long verbatim quotations of Plato's Philebus
summary: Galen quotes Plato's Philebus at length (sound as one and unlimited; grammar and music; colours and figures; pleasures) to show that the arts consist in knowing differences.
quote: The first passage of Plato concerning the constitution of the arts is stated as follows.
note: Phlb. 17b-e, 12e-13a, 12d (outside knowledge). Useful as an indirect witness to Plato's text. At 213 Galen adds the Sophist and the Statesman for the differences of the arts.

title_work: Against Lycus
title: 'τρίτονον' in the Philebus quotation
summary: The Greek reads τρίτονον ὁμότονον where Plato has 'third, the same-pitched'. The draft's 'as a third the equal-toned' follows the right sense.
quote: and as a third the equal-toned
note: Plato Phlb. 17c reads τρίτον ὁμότονον (outside knowledge). τρίτονον looks like a scribal dittography in Kühn's text.

title_work: Against Lycus
title: Galen reduces Lycus' argument by swapping 'hot' for 'sound'
summary: Galen rewrites Lycus' sentence word for word with 'sound' in place of 'hot'. The result would abolish grammar, the art of the 24 letters, and music, so Lycus' argument is invalid too.
quote: it is carried through by means of those very words of his, all of them, with only one, the name of ‘hot’, changed into that of ‘sound’
note: A clear example of Galen's parody-by-substitution method. Musical examples follow: mese, lichanos of the mesai, paramese, parhypate, trite of the diezeugmenai.

title_work: Against Lycus
title: Negation missing or misread in the vowel example
summary: The Greek says Lycus' followers think e is not different from o, 'but o differs (διαφέρειν δὲ) from ō'. The draft renders it as a second negation ('nor does o differ from ō').
quote: nor does o differ from ō
note: The sense needs a negative (οὔτε) and the draft supplies it silently. The transmitted text is probably corrupt here.

title_work: Against Lycus
title: Galen's trilemma on Lycus and the Philebus
summary: If Lycus never read the Philebus, Galen 'admires his education'. If he read it without understanding, he marvels at his intelligence. If he understood but was unpersuaded, he congratulates his judgement.
quote: if Lycus did not read the book at all, I admire Lycus for his education; if he read it but did not understand it, I marvel at his intelligence
note: An ironic rhetorical trilemma typical of Galen's polemic.

title_work: Against Lycus
title: Lycus had partisans who held his views
summary: Galen twice refers to a group who share or champion Lycus' opinions and imagines their objections.
quote: those who champion Lycus’s views will perhaps say
note: Also at 214-215 (οἱ τὰ τοῦ Λύκου φρονοῦντες). This implies that Lycus had a following or readership in Galen's day, though it may be a rhetorical construct.

title_work: Against Lycus
title: Every educated Greek is expected to have read the Philebus
summary: Galen asks whether any Greek physician, grammarian, rhetor or philosopher could not have read the Philebus. He also says Lycus lacks the first lessons taught in the philosophers' schools.
quote: Could there be any Greek man — physician or grammarian or rhetor or philosopher, or in general anyone else at all who lays claim to argument — who has not read Plato’s Philebus?
note: 'ἐν ταῖς φιλοσόφων διατριβαῖς', 'in the schools of the philosophers', is evidence of a common curriculum in dialectic expected of physicians.

title_work: Against Lycus
title: Theophrastus wrote a whole treatise on juice (chylos)
summary: Galen says that on Lycus' view Theophrastus wrote a whole treatise on chylos (juice/flavour) in vain.
quote: in vain wrote a whole treatise on juice (chylos)
note: Diogenes Laertius lists a Theophrastean Περὶ χυλῶν, and CP book 6 treats flavours (outside knowledge). 'Juice' may better be 'flavour' here, since the treatise concerns χυμοί/χυλοί.

title_work: Against Lycus
title: Lycus thought vinegar has a styptic quality
summary: Galen mocks Lycus for holding that vinegar is styptic (astringent) rather than sour: a sign that he ignored flavour distinctions known to materia medica writers.
quote: who has reached such a degree of lack of education as to think that there is a styptic quality in vinegar
note: A specific doctrinal fragment of Lycus. Galen adds sour dock (oxylapathon) and sorrel (oxalis) as sour but not styptic (220-221).

title_work: Against Lycus
title: Dioscorides of Anazarbus and the materia medica writers
summary: Galen says even Dioscorides of Anazarbus and all writers on materia medica knew the flavour distinctions. He lists their nine terms: salty, briny, bitter, sweet, harsh, astringent, styptic, pungent, sour.
quote: For things so evident were known even to Dioscorides of Anazarbus, and to all the others who wrote treatises on materia medica.
note: 'καί ... ἐγίγνωσκεν', 'even Dioscorides', is mildly condescending. The work is 'τὰ περὶ ὕλης ὑπομνήματα'.

title_work: Against Lycus
title: Wine quality: styptic is noble, sour means turning
summary: In wine, stypticity marks excellence. No wine is sour by nature, and any sourness at once raises the suspicion that it is turning to vinegar.
quote: for the styptic wines are of noble quality, whereas none is sour by nature, but if even a little of such a quality comes upon them, we at once suspect their change into vinegar.
note: The same passage notes that apples and pomegranates are popularly called sour, styptic or sweet.

title_work: Against Lycus
title: 'He was acquainted with' the natural philosophers' inquiry on flavours
summary: The Greek reads πάλιν οὖν ἔγνω ('again, then, he knew'). The context requires irony, a question, or a negative ('did he not know').
quote: Again, then, he was acquainted with the inquiry among the natural philosophers about the number of flavours.
note: Possibly corrupt (for example ἠγνόησε). The draft's flat rendering hides the problem.

title_work: Against Lycus
title: Catalogue of named fevers
summary: Galen lists fever kinds that physicians had written about: kausos, leipyria, epialos, typhodes, pestilential, semi-tertian, quotidian, tertian, quartan.
quote: the burning fever (kausos) and the leipyria and the epialos and the typhoid and the pestilential and the semi-tertian, the quotidian and the tertian and the quartan.
note: 'Typhoid' renders τυφώδης and should not be read in the modern sense. The same unit says Lycus 'elsewhere writes of differences of fevers' (ἑτέρωθι γράφει πυρετῶν διαφορὰς).

title_work: Against Lycus
title: Goldworkers use chaff fire (Lycus)
summary: Lycus held that chaff fire is the weakest and is therefore suited to goldworking, since gold melts and runs in a stronger flame. Galen says goldworkers customarily use it.
quote: thinking that the fire of chaff is the weakest, he says that it is serviceable for the working of gold; for the gold, he says, melts and flows away when it comes near a stronger flame.
note: The craft custom is stated at 222-223 (ὡς χρῆσθαι τοῖς τὸν χρυσὸν ἐργαζομένοις ἔθος). The draft's 'serviceable' renders ἐνταμίευτον, a rare and odd word that may be corrupt.

title_work: Against Lycus
title: Galen's physical account of why flames differ
summary: Flame is an exhalation of particles torn from the fuel, with heated air caught between them. The particles differ in size, density and degree of burning, so flames vary.
quote: a certain exhalation arises from the burning material in particles torn apart from one another, between which a certain air is caught
note: He presents this as what Lycus would have learned from the natural philosophers (φυσικῶν φιλοσόφων).

title_work: Against Lycus
title: Lycus' three senses of 'much heat'
summary: Lycus distinguished three senses of 'much heat': by substance, by intensity of the quality, and by strength of its proper activity. He granted growing bodies only the third, and called that usage improper.
quote: he says that ‘much heat’ is understood in one way in respect of substance, in another in respect of the intensification of the quality, and in another in respect of the strength of its proper activity.
note: The core of Lycus' exegesis. Galen later turns all three senses against him (240-241).

title_work: Against Lycus
title: Galen excerpts long quotations rather than copying in full
summary: Galen says Lycus' passage is very long, so, as with the previous one, he copies only the most pertinent part.
quote: for that one too, being extremely long, I did not write out in full, but selected only the most pertinent part of it.
note: Evidence of Galen's quotation practice: the Lycus fragments are selective excerpts.

title_work: Against Lycus
title: Structure of Lycus' comment: two inquiries
summary: In a verbatim quotation Lycus says he set out two questions: whether Hippocrates was right to add 'innate', and whether he was right that heat is greatest in growing things.
quote: one, whether Hippocrates was right to add 'innate', the other, whether he was right to say that the heat is greatest in those who are growing.
note: The quotation seems to run from 226 to about 234. It is the longest surviving piece of Lycus' Aphorisms commentary; the draft's quotation marks should be checked for where it ends.

title_work: Against Lycus
title: Lycus on the works of heat in the body
summary: Within the quotation, Lycus lists heat's works: melting, setting, transforming, and in our bodies digesting food in the stomach and intestines, distributing it, assimilating it, nutrition and growth.
quote: it digests the food in the stomach and the intestines, and conveys the product of its working-up into the body, and alters it into body and attaches it to our bodies, in nutrition and in growth.
note: Lycus' physiology of nutrition and growth closely matches Galen's own scheme. At 229-230 Lycus holds the strongest heat is the most well-proportioned (τὸ μάλιστα σύμμετρον), not the most intense.

title_work: Against Lycus
title: 'οὐκ ἂν' where 'even if' is required
summary: The Greek reads οἷον τὸ πῦρ οὐκ ἂν ἐπ’ ὀλίγης οὐσίας θεωρεῖται. The draft renders 'even if it is observed in a small amount', which presupposes κἂν.
quote: as for instance fire, even if it is observed in a small amount of substance
note: The check failed for this unit. The draft's sense is probably right, but the transmitted Greek seems corrupt (οὐκ ἂν for κἂν).

title_work: Against Lycus
title: Lycus attacks the proof in On the Nature of Man
summary: In the quotation, Lycus calls 'utterly foolish' the proof in the treatise On the Nature of Man that heat is greatest in the young, because nourishment is carried upward against its weight during growth.
quote: For what is said by him in the treatise On the Nature of Man, as a proof that heat is greatest in those who are growing, is utterly foolish
note: The speaker is Lycus, and 'him' is Hippocrates. At 233-234 Lycus grants the same passage 'would have been well said' in the third sense. The Ionic βίην there suggests a verbatim Hippocratic quotation, which needs locating in the extant text.

title_work: Against Lycus
title: Draft supplies '[not]' absent from the Greek
summary: The Greek reads τῇ μὲν οὖν φωνῇ δοκοίη ἂν καλῶς κεχρῆσθαι ('would seem to have used the word well'). The logic, and Galen's summary at 234, require 'not well'.
quote: as regards the expression he would seem [not] to have used it well, because he said the heat is greatest when he ought to have said strongest
note: The check failed for this unit. The draft's bracketed supplement is justified: read οὐ καλῶς.

title_work: Against Lycus
title: Lycus: a child has a bigger brain than an elephant, proportionally
summary: Galen cites Lycus' own claim from elsewhere that man has the largest brain relative to body size. A small child has a larger brain than the largest elephant by proportion, so Lycus should have judged heat proportionally too.
quote: he says in this way that a small child has a larger brain than the largest elephant, attending not to the bulk of the body alone but adding to it the consideration according to proportion
note: An anatomical fragment of Lycus (ἑτέρωθι, 'elsewhere'), relevant to his reputation as an anatomist (outside knowledge).

title_work: Against Lycus
title: 'Innate' means primordial: the body from seed and menses
summary: Galen glosses 'innate' as 'primordial' (archegonon): the body present from the beginning, from which the animal was first generated, namely menstrual blood and seed.
quote: having considered what sort of thing among the bodies in us is innate, that is, primordial.
note: At 235-236 he invokes Hippocrates' 'six-day seed' (τὴν ἑκταίαν γονὴν), in which only the innate hot body exists before bone, vein or nerve form.

title_work: Against Lycus
title: Embryo: blood-clot flesh with 'blood-weals'
summary: The earliest embryo is unformed soft flesh like a blood clot, containing what Hippocrates called 'blood-weals'. Outlines of bone, cartilage, nerve and vessels form later, and the innate hot body shrinks relative to acquired parts.
quote: For a certain unformed soft flesh, resembling a clot of blood, takes over the first appearance of the embryo, having within it certain things, as Hippocrates named them, like blood-weals
note: Hippocratic Nat. Puer. (outside knowledge). Greek οἶον is a misaccented οἷον. In extreme old age animals are nearly all bone, nerve, membrane and vessel; only flesh is bloody, and the old have little of it.

title_work: Against Lycus
title: Cites his commentaries On Seed
summary: Galen says he showed in his commentaries On Seed that seed, made of serous moisture and pneuma, is least in the old and greatest in the young.
quote: as we demonstrated in the commentaries On Seed.
note: Extant De semine (Kühn IV). The reference gives a relative date: On Seed predates this text.

title_work: Against Lycus
title: Wine-mixing measures: kotyle, pithos, kyathoi
summary: To illustrate proportion, Galen contrasts a kotyle of water thrown into a jar (pithos) of wine with a small cup of three kyathoi, one of water and two of wine.
quote: having thrown a cotyle of water into a jar of wine, he says that the water in the jar is more than that in a small cup, when, as it happens, there are three cyathi in the latter
note: A 1:2 water-to-wine cup is mentioned in passing. Drinkers judge the mix by proportion, not volume.

title_work: Against Lycus
title: Tetrapharmakon recipe: wax, fat, pitch, resin in equal parts
summary: Galen uses the tetrapharmakon, equal parts wax, fat, pitch and resin, to show that 'more pitch' means more by proportion, not by the size of the vessel.
quote: the preparation called the tetrapharmakon, composed of wax and fat and pitch and resin, all put together in equal amounts
note: 'δύναμις' here means a compound drug. The recipe matches standard ancient tetrapharmakon (outside knowledge).

title_work: Against Lycus
title: A common drug of iris, aristolochia, vetch flour, frankincense
summary: Galen describes a very customary drug of iris, aristolochia, bitter-vetch flour and frankincense in equal weights. Doubling the aristolochia makes it 'more' in substance, quality and activity.
quote: this drug, which is among the most customary, and which is composed of iris and aristolochia and the flour of bitter vetch and frankincense, all equal to one another in weight
note: Here the ingredients are not wholly blended, unlike the tetrapharmakon.

title_work: Against Lycus
title: 'Throughout the whole book' probably 'throughout all of life'
summary: Galen says this loose usage ('more' for 'more intense') is extremely common 'throughout the whole book and in all the arts'. ἐν ὅλῳ τῷ βιβλίῳ makes poor sense; βίῳ ('life') would fit.
quote: though such a use of the words is extremely common throughout the whole book and in all the arts.
note: The check failed for this unit. The probable emendation βιβλίῳ to βίῳ fits the following appeal to everyday speech about fevers.

title_work: Against Lycus
title: Galen's verdict: Lycus untaught, a corrupter of the young
summary: Galen concludes that Hippocrates erred in nothing. Lycus was never introduced to the Hippocratic doctrines by teachers, contradicts himself, and corrupts the young who lack logical training.
quote: you have not been introduced at all by teachers so as to understand anything of the Hippocratic doctrines
note: 'λυμαινόμενος τοῖς νέοις' echoes the charge against Socrates. Galen stresses formal instruction by teachers as the qualification for an exegete.
